title: Put JPG images on A4 PDF pages
description: Make a printable A4 PDF from JPG or PNG images with a consistent page size and visible margins.
intro: Use this workflow when a printer or recipient asks for A4 pages rather than photo-sized pages. A4 fixes the paper size at 210 × 297 mm; it does not improve the resolution of the source photograph. A wide photograph on a portrait page will leave unused space because keeping the full image and filling every edge are different goals.
settings: Portrait for uniform upright sheets; Landscape for wide drawings
Small or Big when content must stay away from paper edges
Merge enabled: one page per image in one PDF
steps: Add JPG or PNG files and remove duplicates before converting. Files are processed in the browser; a local selection does not upload the photos.
Choose A4 in Page size. Choose Portrait if all sheets must face the same way; Auto can orient pages differently for portrait and landscape images.
Choose a margin and inspect the preview. Rotate a sideways source image using its card control, then drag the cards into reading order.
Convert and open the downloaded PDF. Check its page size and use the printer’s preview to decide between actual size and fit to printable area.
checks: Page properties show A4 dimensions, with width and height exchanged only for landscape pages.
The last line, signature and any content near the edge remain visible.
The PDF page count matches the selected image count.
limitation: The converter cannot restore blurred text or promise borderless printing. Printer hardware and driver settings still determine the printable area.
question: Does A4 stretch the picture?
answer: The image is fitted to the available page area. If its aspect ratio differs from the page, unused space is expected; inspect the preview before exporting.

title: Put JPG images on US Letter PDF pages
description: Create a US Letter PDF from images with deliberate orientation and margins for a Letter-based printing workflow.
intro: Choose this workflow when a recipient specifies US Letter, not simply because a person lives in a particular country. Letter measures 8.5 × 11 inches and differs from A4. Selecting the correct size in the converter avoids relying on a printer to scale an A4 file later, which can change apparent text size.
settings: Portrait or Landscape according to the page content
JPG/JPEG and PNG; up to 100 MB per file
steps: Select the images in JPG to PDF. If a camera saved a different format, export a JPG or PNG copy before adding it.
Set Page size to US Letter. Set a fixed orientation if the recipient requires every page to use the same orientation.
Choose a small or large margin and inspect the page edges. Reorder or rotate image cards before starting conversion.
Download and open the PDF in a viewer. Confirm Letter in page properties, then check the print preview on the actual target printer.
checks: Page size is Letter rather than A4.
Small labels remain readable at the intended printed size.
No receipt or signature is hidden by a page edge.
limitation: Changing paper size is a layout decision, not image enhancement. Small source photos will not gain detail, and conversion does not perform OCR.
question: Should I choose Letter or A4?
answer: Use the size required by the recipient or printer. There is no need to create two versions unless both paper sizes are actually needed.

title: Convert transparent PNG artwork to PDF
description: Place PNG artwork into PDF pages and check transparency, white backgrounds and fine edges before printing.
intro: Transparent PNGs can look different against a checkerboard, a dark application theme and a white PDF page. This workflow helps distinguish a viewer background from missing artwork. Keep the original PNG so you can compare visible edges and colors after conversion; a PDF preview is not a replacement for checking the exported file.
settings: PNG, including files with an alpha channel
Fit for image-sized output; A4 or Letter for paper layouts
The PNG is embedded through the PDF image library
A white PDF page in a separate PDF viewer
steps: Choose the original PNG rather than a screenshot of its preview. Avoid converting to JPG first if transparent edges matter.
Set Fit and Auto for an image-sized page, or choose the paper size required by the recipient. Add a margin if artwork must be inset.
Convert and open the actual PDF. Inspect light logos and translucent shadows on the white page, not only in the website’s dark theme.
If the intended design needs a colored background, add that background in your image editor and export a new PNG, then convert that copy.
checks: Light artwork has enough contrast on the intended page background.
Edges and shadows are not confused with the viewer’s display background.
All artwork is inside the page bounds.
limitation: PDFPilot does not add a background editor or guarantee print color matching. A transparent image and white artwork can look blank on white paper even when present.
question: Does dark mode change my PDF background?
answer: The website theme is interface styling. Choose and inspect the document’s content independently; dark mode is not an artwork background setting.

title: Make a separate PDF for each JPG or PNG
description: Convert a group of images into individual PDF files in a ZIP instead of merging every image into one PDF.
intro: Separate PDFs are useful when each photograph, scanned receipt or form belongs to a different record. The important control is the merge checkbox: it changes the output grouping, not the picture content. This workflow avoids creating a merged PDF and then splitting it simply to recover one file per image.
settings: Merge all images in one PDF
Orientation, size and margin still apply
steps: Add the JPG or PNG files. Remove unwanted images and inspect their rotations before deciding how to group the output.
Turn off Merge all images in one PDF. Keep the option on only when the recipient wants a single multi-page document.
Choose page size, orientation and margin. Review the preview because every individual PDF uses the chosen layout options.
Convert, save the ZIP, extract it locally and open a sample from the beginning and end. Check file names before attaching documents to separate records.
checks: The downloaded file is a ZIP and extracts without errors.
The number of PDFs equals the number of selected images.
Each PDF contains the correct image, not an assumed file order.
limitation: An archive is a download container, not a combined PDF. Some recipient systems do not accept ZIP files; extract and send the individual PDFs when necessary.
question: Will disabling merge remove an image?
answer: No. It changes how results are packaged. Remove an image from the selection if it should not be converted.

title: Convert a DOCX with tables to PDF
description: Convert Word tables in the browser and review long rows, borders and page breaks in the image-based PDF.
intro: Tables are more demanding than plain paragraphs because column widths, merged cells and page breaks interact. This workflow is for a DOCX that already contains the table; PDFPilot does not provide a table editor. The browser renderer includes supported tables, but its pagination is not the same engine used by Microsoft Word.
settings: Up to 200 pages; 100 MB per file
steps: Save a DOCX copy with the intended page size and table widths. If the document originated elsewhere, inspect that exported DOCX first.
Select the document in Word to PDF. Keep the original file available so you can compare the first, middle and last table rows.
Convert and expand the page previews. Pay particular attention to tables that continue across pages and unusually tall cells.
Download and inspect the PDF in a viewer. If rows are clipped or pagination is unacceptable, adjust the source table or export directly from the original editor.
checks: All columns and the final row are present.
Borders, cell shading and merged headings are understandable.
Page breaks do not separate content in a misleading way.
limitation: This creates a visual PDF, not an accessible or searchable table structure. Use the original editor’s export when tagged tables, selectable text or exact Word pagination are required.
question: Can I copy table cells from this PDF?
answer: Not as a native table from this browser output: pages are images. Keep the DOCX or use a native editor export when text extraction is required.

title: Convert a DOCX with embedded pictures to PDF
description: Keep supported embedded images in a browser-generated PDF and check image placement alongside surrounding text.
intro: A picture visible in an editor may be embedded in the DOCX archive or linked to a separate resource. Those are not equivalent inputs. PDFPilot keeps conversion local and does not fetch private remote image URLs to fill gaps. Start with a self-contained DOCX so the browser has the content it needs.
settings: No remote document-asset upload or retrieval workflow
Placement, crop, captions and page breaks
steps: Open the source document and save a DOCX copy with pictures embedded. Do not assume a link to a picture contains the picture data.
Choose the DOCX in Word to PDF. If the converter reports unsupported content, read the error and return to the original editor.
Convert and review all pages containing pictures. Compare the picture itself, its crop and the text or caption that follows it.
Download and check the PDF separately before sharing. Keep the source DOCX for edits; the output is not intended to remain an editable Word layout.
checks: Every expected embedded picture is present.
Captions belong to the correct pictures.
No picture or caption is clipped at a page boundary.
limitation: Unsupported drawing objects and embedded media are not promised to render. Fonts and page breaks can differ. The resulting page text is not selectable or searchable.
question: Will a web image link automatically become a picture?
answer: No. Embed the picture in the DOCX first, or export from the original editor. A hyperlink by itself is not image data.

title: Convert a Google Docs DOCX export to PDF
description: Use a downloaded DOCX from Google Docs with the browser converter and distinguish export changes from conversion changes.
intro: This workflow starts with a DOCX file already saved from Google Docs. PDFPilot is not connected to your Drive account and does not read a shared document URL. There are two transformations to check: Google Docs to DOCX, then DOCX to PDF. A missing picture in the intermediate DOCX cannot be recovered by the second step.
settings: Prefer the original editor’s PDF export
steps: Download a Word-compatible DOCX copy from Google Docs and keep the original document unchanged.
Open or inspect that DOCX before conversion. Confirm pictures, tables and page size survived the export to Word format.
Select the local DOCX in Word to PDF, convert it and review the generated pages, especially content near page breaks.
If exact Google Docs appearance or selectable PDF text matters, use Google Docs’ own PDF export instead and compare the result before distributing it.
checks: The intermediate DOCX contains the expected pictures and tables.
The PDF includes the complete document, including the final page.
Fonts, page breaks and clickable links meet the recipient’s needs.
limitation: This is file conversion, not a live Google Docs integration. Browser-local rendering cannot guarantee identical layout across editors.
question: Can I paste a Google Docs sharing link here?
answer: No. This tool accepts local DOCX files. Download a DOCX first, or use the source editor’s direct PDF export.

title: Convert multiple DOCX documents to separate PDFs
description: Process several Word documents locally and download one PDF per document in a ZIP archive.
intro: Batch conversion saves repeated file selection when each Word document needs its own PDF. It does not merge all documents into one publication. Documents are processed sequentially to limit simultaneous rendering work, so completion time depends on the page count, image sizes and the available memory on your device.
settings: One PDF per DOCX, bundled as ZIP
100 MB per document; up to 200 pages per document
steps: Select the DOCX documents you need and remove unrelated files. Inspect names so you can match each result to its source.
Arrange or rotate documents as needed. This ordering is a review aid; each selected document still becomes a separate PDF.
Start conversion and keep the tab open. If you cancel or an error occurs, do not treat a partial or missing archive as a completed batch.
Extract the ZIP and review every PDF. Check the first and last page of each document, then inspect image-heavy pages and long tables.
checks: Every selected document has a corresponding PDF.
Every PDF opens and has a plausible page count.
The correct output file is used for each recipient.
limitation: Image-based PDFs can be larger than the source DOCX. Batch output is not a guarantee that every advanced Word object is supported or that all layouts match Word exactly.
question: Does the batch become one PDF?
answer: No. Word batch conversion creates separate PDFs in an archive. The originals remain unchanged.

title: Convert PPTX vector drawings to PDF
description: Convert supported slide paths, grouped drawings, pictures and text, then inspect linework at high zoom.
intro: Technical slides often contain thousands of tiny paths rather than one large picture. Treating only text boxes and photographs as content loses important drawing information. PDFPilot’s PPTX renderer handles supported custom paths, groups and transforms, but a successful export still needs a visual check against the source presentation.
settings: PPTX with supported DrawingML shapes and paths
Slide edges, group alignment and fine linework
steps: Save the presentation as PPTX and keep a reference view in its original editor. Check that any externally linked assets are embedded.
Choose the PPTX in PowerPoint to PDF. The slide dimensions come from the presentation rather than an A4 print setting.
Convert while watching the progress indicator. If unsupported content produces an error, use the original editor rather than accepting a simplified missing-content version.
Open the PDF and zoom into dense drawing regions. Compare line endpoints, rotated groups, labels, image crops and the final slide.
checks: Thin lines and dense drawing groups are present.
Rotated or scaled groups line up with their labels.
Small text and symbols remain legible.
limitation: Font substitution and text wrapping may differ. This is not a CAD validator or an exact PowerPoint rendering guarantee; use native export for contractual drawing deliverables that require exact appearance.
question: Are supported vector drawings turned into a screenshot?
answer: The renderer writes supported drawing paths into the PDF. Embedded photos remain images, and text depends on available font support.

title: Convert widescreen PPTX slides to PDF
description: Keep a widescreen presentation’s slide dimensions in PDF instead of squeezing slides onto portrait paper.
intro: A slide is a document page with its own size. A widescreen deck is usually intended to retain its wide layout when shared on screens. The converter reads presentation dimensions; printer paper selection is a later decision. A white margin introduced by a print dialog does not necessarily mean the PDF changed the slide size.
settings: Optional document rotation in the workspace
steps: Check the slide size in the source presentation and save the PPTX. Confirm whether the deck is actually widescreen or uses a custom size.
Add it to PowerPoint to PDF. Avoid rotating the whole file unless the entire document needs a quarter-turn.
Convert and open the PDF. Inspect page dimensions and compare the first slide with the source, especially objects close to the edges.
When printing, choose appropriate paper orientation and scaling in the print dialog. Keep the screen-sharing PDF separately if a paper-specific version is required.
checks: PDF aspect ratio matches the source slide dimensions.
Full-width backgrounds and edge objects are visible.
The slide count and PDF page count agree.
limitation: Keeping page dimensions does not guarantee matching fonts, text wrapping or unsupported Office effects. Check those separately before sharing.
question: Does the converter force A4 pages?
answer: No. PPTX conversion uses presentation slide dimensions. The A4 and Letter controls belong to JPG to PDF, not the PPTX tool.

title: Check fonts when converting PPTX to PDF
description: Understand font substitution, missing glyph errors and text wrapping before sharing a browser-converted presentation.
intro: Matching the font name is not sufficient to guarantee the same text layout across applications. Glyph coverage, font metrics and line wrapping also affect how labels fit inside shapes. This workflow separates readable text from exact typography so you can choose the appropriate export path for a design-sensitive presentation.
settings: PDF text drawn with supported available fonts
Unsupported font coverage can stop conversion
Use the original editor’s PDF export
steps: Identify slides with branded fonts, mathematical symbols or non-Latin text. Keep a reference view from the original presentation.
Convert the PPTX locally. If a font or glyph error appears, note the affected content rather than assuming it was safely omitted.
Compare line breaks, bullets, superscripts, symbols and labels in narrow boxes. Zoom in; checking only the slide thumbnail can miss displaced text.
If typography is essential, export PDF from PowerPoint with the intended fonts available. Recheck that PDF on another viewer before sending it.
checks: Every symbol and character is visible.
Text does not overflow its shape or overlap nearby objects.
Titles and labels retain an acceptable hierarchy.
limitation: Browser conversion does not guarantee that proprietary or embedded Office fonts will be used exactly. It cannot add a missing font license or reconstruct an absent glyph.
question: Will installing a font always make browser output identical?
answer: No. Font availability is only one factor; layout and rendering behavior can still differ. Native export is the appropriate reference for exact typography.

title: Export PPTX charts and SmartArt safely to PDF
description: Choose a safe export path when a presentation includes charts, SmartArt or other content the browser converter cannot render.
intro: A converter should not report success after silently removing the most important chart on a slide. PDFPilot’s browser renderer rejects supported categories of known unsupported content instead of promising a faithful chart export. This workflow helps you decide whether to simplify a copy or use the original editor; it is not a claim of chart support.
settings: Not supported by this browser converter
Conversion error rather than intentional silent omission
PDF export from PowerPoint or the original editor
steps: Inspect the source deck for charts, SmartArt, video and embedded objects. Do not rely on a filename or file size to identify these features.
Use the original editor’s PDF export when you need its complete visual appearance. Review static PDF output because animations and interactive content are not the same as a slide show.
If you deliberately simplify a copy, replace complex objects with static pictures in the source editor and clearly retain the original presentation.
Convert only the compatible copy in the browser, then compare every altered slide. Check labels, legends and data values as well as the picture outline.
checks: No chart, legend or data label is missing.
A static picture is acceptable for the intended recipient.
The original editable chart and presentation remain available.
limitation: Do not remove an error guard to force a download. PDF is a static document workflow here; video playback, animations and editable chart data are not promised.
question: Can I ignore the unsupported-content error?
answer: No. Use native export or deliberately prepare a compatible copy and review it. Retrying unchanged unsupported content does not establish correctness.
